claims.text: Melt-spinning Cr16Mn16Fe16Co16Ni16P20 at cooling rates of approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s produces an amorphous structure.
A single reheating pulse above 1000 K/s immediately after melt-spinning will enhance amorphous retention.
A single reheating pulse above 1000 K/s immediately after melt-spinning will enhance the alloy's thermal stability.
Ultrafast reheating can bypass a critical temperature window for nucleation of primary crystalline phases.
Approximately 960–1291 K is a crystallization-temperature window identified for this alloy by DSC and thermal analysis.
The cited 960 K and 1291 K transformation temperatures define a critical reheating window that should be traversed rapidly.
Slow cooling produces a complex crystalline microstructure containing FCC A and multiple tetragonal and orthorhombic phases.
Accelerated cooling at about 3018 K/s produces fewer phases than slow cooling.
The alloy undergoes FCC and eutectic crystallization at cooling-condition-dependent temperatures, including approximately 1341 K and 960 K under accelerated cooling.
Conventional slower reheating causes multistep crystallization with extensive primary-phase formation in this alloy.
Minimizing dwell time in phase-forming temperature ranges preserves the short-range atomic order of the amorphous phase.
The melt-spun alloy exhibits short-range atomic order characteristic of a metallic glass.
Ultrafast reheating kinetically hinders crystallization by reducing the time available for atomic rearrangement into nucleation clusters.
The reheating pulse permits limited structural relaxation that increases thermal stability without substantial crystallization.
Compared with conventional reheating or no additional intervention, the pulse will produce a higher retained amorphous fraction.
Compared with conventional reheating or no additional intervention, the pulse will delay crystallization onset during subsequent thermal analysis.
Cooling at approximately 10^5–10^6 K/s is an effective boundary for obtaining the amorphous starting state, whereas substantially slower cooling promotes crystalline phase formation.
Reheating too slowly through 960–1291 K will cause primary crystallization.
The exact reheating-rate threshold required to suppress primary crystallization is not established.
